//: Cotton and alfalfa. Agronomic entries are scoped by deviceNamePattern to placeholders (%cotton%, %alfalfa%) — rename devices to match or replace the pattern with deviceProfiles before trusting an alert. Thresholds are the published extension figures cited in each entry; they are starting points, not calibrations.
//months: activeMonths are US Cotton Belt timing (planting April–May, bloom July–August). The San Joaquin Valley plants from about March 10.
//enabled: Enabled: checks whose threshold is a published figure the sensor measures directly — air, leaf and soil temperature, humidity, durations, rates, pH. Disabled: checks whose threshold depends on this soil or this probe (volumetric moisture, EC, N, the 'wet' cut-off of a leaf-wetness sensor) or that need the forecast block — each says what to set before enabling it.

checks.//: ═══ FLEET HEALTH — every pack carries these, so the pack runs on its own. None needs crop tuning. ═══

SOIL WARM ENOUGH TO PLANT. K-State and LSU: 18.3 °C (65 °F) at 4 in, read at 8 a.m., for 3 consecutive days, with a 5-day forecast of at least 25–26 DD60 and lows staying above 10 °C (50 °F). 8 a.m. is near the daily soil minimum, so requiring the probe to stay above 18.3 °C unbroken for 72 h is a close, slightly stricter reading of the same rule. Needs a probe at 4 in. California (UC IPM) is lower: soil at seed depth above 58 °F (14.4 °C). Sources: K-State eUpdate 588, https://eupdate.agronomy.ksu.edu/article/soil-temperature-weather-forecast-and-seed-quality-are-critical-for-cotton-establishment-588-3 ; UC IPM cotton planting forecast, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/weather/cotton-planting-forecast/

COLD NIGHT IN THE 5-DAY FORECAST at planting. K-State and LSU: postpone planting unless lows stay above 10 °C (50 °F) through the 5-day forecast. DISABLED: needs the top-level forecast block and a Weatherbit key (see README, Forecast).

COOL SPELL AFTER PLANTING. UC IPM rates a 5-day DD60 total of 10 °F-days or less as unfavourable for emergence (16–20 adequate, over 20 ideal); emergence needs 50–80 DD60. DD60 is (Tmax+Tmin)/2 − 60 °F with no upper cap. This computes the °C equivalent (base 15.6 °C; 10 °F-days = 5.6 °C-days) by integrating the hourly curve rather than from daily max/min, which reads a little higher on days that barely clear the base. Sources: UC IPM cotton planting forecast, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/weather/cotton-planting-forecast/ ; UC IPM cotton DD table, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/WEATHER/DDTABLE/cotton.html

HEAT AT FLOWERING. Cotton Foundation: days above 35 °C (95 °F) with nights above 27 °C substantially increase boll shed; pollen germination falls above 28 °C and fails at 37 °C. Shed shows 4–5 days after the heat starts. Source: "Stress Physiology in Cotton", ch. 1, https://cotton.org/foundation/upload/Stress-Physiology-in-Cotton_Chapter1.pdf

HOT NIGHT at peak bloom: a night minimum above 26.7 °C (80 °F) causes heavy shed of small bolls (Cotton Physiology Today, https://www.cotton.org/tech/physiology/cpt/plantphysiology/upload/cpt-july90-repop.pdf).

ROOT-ZONE SALINITY — cotton: Maas–Hoffman threshold ECe 7.7 dS/m, above which yield declines. DISABLED until converted to what the probe reads. Maas–Hoffman thresholds are saturated-paste ECe. A soil probe reports bulk EC (or pore EC), which is not ECe: FAO 29 gives soil-water EC ≈ 2 × ECe at field capacity, and bulk EC is lower than pore EC and moves with water content. Convert before enabling — take a saturated-paste lab sample beside the probe and scale this threshold by the probe/ECe ratio. Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, ch. 2 and Annex 1 (Maas & Grattan 1999), https://www.fao.org/4/t0234e/t0234e02.htm , https://www.fao.org/4/y4263e/y4263e0e.htm

SOIL pH — cotton: outside 5.8–8.0. Mississippi State: "Cotton grows best in soil with a pH between 5.8 and 7.0"; yield losses are usually not severe until pH drops below 5.5 on sandy and silt loams (5.2 on clay loams) — lower min to 5.5 if the alert should mean yield loss rather than drift off optimum. SERA-6 finds the yield plateau from about 5.8. No cotton-specific upper limit was found; 8.0 is this pack's choice (NMSU, general: most crops do well at 6.2–8.3, sodium problems from 8.5). pH moves over seasons, not hours, so this is info and needs a day sustained. Sources: Mississippi State, https://extension.msstate.edu/publications/inorganic-nutrient-management-for-cotton-production-mississippi ; SERA-6 Bull. 410, https://aesl.ces.uga.edu/sera6/PUB/sera6-cotton-pub.pdf ; NMSU CR-676, https://pubs.nmsu.edu/_circulars/CR676/index.html

ALFALFA WEEVIL. Degree-days above 48 °F (8.9 °C) from January 1. Begin scouting at 200 °F-days in southern Iowa, 250 in northern Iowa and Ohio, 300 in Wisconsin (UW, sine method); egg hatch near 300 and peak larval feeding near 575. Keep the milestone for your region and delete the others. Sources: ISU, "Alfalfa weevil", https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/alfalfa-weevil ; UW AgWeather, https://agweather.cals.wisc.edu/thermal-models/alfalfa-weevil

ROOT-ZONE SALINITY — alfalfa: Maas–Hoffman threshold ECe 2.0 dS/m, above which yield declines. DISABLED until converted to what the probe reads. Maas–Hoffman thresholds are saturated-paste ECe. A soil probe reports bulk EC (or pore EC), which is not ECe: FAO 29 gives soil-water EC ≈ 2 × ECe at field capacity, and bulk EC is lower than pore EC and moves with water content. Convert before enabling — take a saturated-paste lab sample beside the probe and scale this threshold by the probe/ECe ratio. Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, ch. 2 and Annex 1 (Maas & Grattan 1999), https://www.fao.org/4/t0234e/t0234e02.htm , https://www.fao.org/4/y4263e/y4263e0e.htm

SOIL pH — alfalfa: outside 6.5–7.5. pH moves over seasons, not hours, so this is info and needs a day sustained; it stays open until the field is limed or acidified. Source: Wisconsin A2809, https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/nutrient-application-guidelines-for-field-vegetable-and-fruit-crops-in-wisconsin-a2809/soil-ph-and-lime-requirement/
